StringWithMarkup.String:
General Background

1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE is a commercially important alkaloid produced by some plants (see pathways PWY-5037 and PWY-5038).  1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE degradation pathways have been reported in yeast, filamentous fungi, some plants (see pathways PWY-6552 and PWY-6553), bacteria and animals.  Although the overall scheme of demethylation and oxidation reactions is similar, the main pathways, enzymes used, and some of the products vary.  In humans 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE is degraded by cytochrome P-450, N-acetyltransferase and xanthine oxidase enzymes [PMID: 15013152], whereas the bacterial pathways appear to involve enzymes different from these.  The bacterial enzymes are of interest in bioremediation of 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE-containing waste from coffee and tea processing, the conversion of such waste to animal feed, the development of biodecaffination techniques, as well as their use in the development of pharmaceuticals and biofuels.  Although these pathways are relatively well characterized, the demethylation enzymes have generally been unstable during purification. Work on gene cloning and recombinant enzyme purification and characterization is in progress [PMID: 22328667]. Reviewed in [14977550] [17009088] and [PMID: 8919637].

Although 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE in high concentrations is toxic to bacteria, some develop the ability to catabolize it.  This includes strains of TAX-286 and TAX-507 and an unnamed strain of TAX-615 [MAZZA96]). 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE-degrading strains have been isolated from the soil under coffee trees and in the laboratory by enrichment procedures involving 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE addition to the growth media.  1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE-degrading bacteria use both N-demethylation and oxidation for 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE catabolism, as shown in this pathway and in pathways PWY-6538 and PWY-6632.  In the N-demethylating pathway, 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE is thought to be initially degraded by an oxidative demethylation mechanism.  This mechanism involves N-demethylating monooxygenases that utilize NAD(P)H, producing dimethylxanthines, followed by monomethylxanthines and XANTHINE.  This mechanism has been supported by the creation of EC 1.14.13.128.  XANTHINE is degraded by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to URATE, which is then degraded as shown in the pathway link.  In these reactions the methyl groups are oxidized to FORMALDEHYDE. 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE and its derivatives may also be oxidized by caffeine oxidases or dehydrogenases to their corresponding methylurate derivatives as shown in this pathway and pathway PWY-6632 (reviewed in [PMID: 14977550] and [PMID: 17009088]).

Although most studies report an oxidative demethylation mechanism for 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE and its derivatives as shown here, an early study by [PMID: 1158847] proposed a hydrolytic demethylation mechanism (not shown).  It was suggested that 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE is metabolized by a demethylating enzyme capable of hydrolyzing each of the three methyl groups and converting them to METOH.  METOH was proposed to be oxidized by dehydrogenases to CARBON-DIOXIDE via FORMALDEHYDE and FORMATE (reviewed in [14977550] [17009088].

Bacteria have not been reported to demethylate 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE to CPD-12479 (1,3-dimethylxanthine), a reaction found in 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE-degrading fungi and plants (reviewed in [PMID: 14977550]) (see pathway PWY-6552).  However, it has been shown that ORG-6144 was able to utilize CPD-12479 and 3-METHYLXANTHINE as sole carbon and nitrogen source, in addition to 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE, 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE, 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE and 7-METHYLXANTHINE.  CPD-12479 and 3-METHYLXANTHINE were metabolized to XANTHINE via N-demethylation.  CPD-12479 and its 3-METHYLXANTHINE and CPD-9025 derivatives were also metabolized by oxidation to methylurates although these did not appear to be further metabolized.  Growth of ORG-6144 on either 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE, CPD-12479, or the N-demethylated metabolites of 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE resulted in coexpression of enzymes involved in the N-demethylation pathways of both 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE and CPD-12479 [PMID: 19447909].  More recently, enzymes degrading both 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE and CPD-12479 have been characterized [22328667][20966097] (see pathway PWY-6999).

The inducible nature of 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE-degrading enzymes in TAX-286 strains has been demonstrated [18720498] [7461603].  Recent studies of 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE degradation done with whole cells, or cell-free extracts include [20495941] [19229573] [19447909] [18720498] [17554468].  Reviewed in [PMID: 17009088].

About This Pathway

1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE can be oxidized directly by caffeine oxidase or caffeine dehydrogenase to CPD-12480.  Caffeine oxidase has been reported in ORG-6150 [PMID: 16647778] and in a mixed culture consortium of TAX-570 and TAX-1827 [9705852] [10491316].  In the mixed culture consortium CPD-12480 was further metabolized to CPD-12485 and then to CPD-12484 (not shown) [PMID: 9705852].  A novel caffeine dehydrogenase has been characterized in TAX-765715 [PMID: 17981969].

Subsequent work using TAX-765715 demonstrated the conversion of CPD-12480 to CPD-16697 catalyzed by a novel NADH-dependent trimethyluric acid monooxygenase encoded by gene tmuM. The CPD-16697 product of TmuM was proposed to either spontaneously decomposes to racemic CPD-12485 through a CPD-16698 intermediate, or be enzymatically converted to CPD-16699 by a putative TmuH hydrolase and a putative TmuD decarboxylase (see below). The further metabolism of CPD-16699 remains to be determined |CITS: 22609920|.

Based on sequence similarities, two nearby genes tmuH encoding a putative 1,3,7-trimethyl-5-hydroxyisourate hydrolase, and tmuD encoding a putative 3,6,8-trimethyl-2-oxo-4-hydroxy-4-carboxy-5-ureidoimidazoline decarboxylase were also identified. Together, the combined enzymological analysis of recombiant TmuM, homology analyses of TmuH and TmuD, and metabolite analyses by ESI-LC-MS, and NMR allowed a pathway for caffeine degradation via CPD-12480 to CPD-16699 to be proposed (this pathway) [PMID: 22609920].

In some other 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE-degrading bacteria the major route of 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) catabolism appears to be via initial demethylation to 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE (3,7-dimethylxanthine), followed by demethylation to 7-METHYLXANTHINE, and then XANTHINE.  Another route of 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE degradation is via initial demethylation to 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE (1,7-dimethylxanthine) followed by 7-METHYLXANTHINE and XANTHINE.  In these reports, oxidation of methylxanthines to their corresponding methyluric acids was not demonstrated (see pathway PWY-6538).  Reviewed in [PMID: 17009088].

ORG-6145 was shown to degrade caffeine by the demethylation pathway, but it also oxidized 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE, 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE and 7-METHYLXANTHINE to their corresponding methyluric acids via a broad substrate specificity CPLX-8094.  The methyluric acids did not support growth of the organism [YAMAOKA99] (see pathway PWY-6632).
